title: Visuospatial Neglect: Theory-Informed Rehabilitation Strategies and the Emerging Therapeutic Role of Non-invasive Brain Stimulation

subsections.section_title: Conceptual and Clinical Foundations of Visuospatial Neglect
subsections.content:
Visuospatial neglect is a neuropsychological syndrome in which patients fail to orient, report, or respond to stimuli on the side of space contralateral to a brain lesion, despite primary sensory and motor pathways being relatively preserved. Classically associated with right hemisphere damage and left-sided neglect, it is now understood not as a unitary visual deficit but as a disorder of spatial attention, representation, and action that can affect perception, exploration, and goal-directed behavior across multiple reference frames ref [1], ref [2].

Core phenomenology is heterogeneous. Neglect may involve personal, peripersonal, or extrapersonal space; manifest in sensory, representational, or motor-intentional domains; and appear in egocentric or allocentric coordinates. Patients may omit left-sided items on cancellation or copying tasks, bisect lines rightward of center, ignore people or objects on the contralesional side, or even neglect the left side of internal mental images ref [2], ref [3]. This multidimensionality is one reason why bedside presentation and test performance can vary substantially across tasks and contexts.

A related defining feature is the frequent dissociation between neglect and elementary visual loss. Unlike hemianopia, neglect reflects a pathological spatial bias in selection and awareness, often accompanied by poor spontaneous compensation and, in some cases, reduced insight into deficits (anosognosia). Contemporary accounts therefore frame neglect as a syndrome arising from disruption of distributed attention and spatial cognition networks rather than from isolated sensory damage ref [1], ref [4].

subsections.section_title: Conceptual and Clinical Foundations of Visuospatial Neglect
subsections.content:
Clinically, visuospatial neglect is not a unitary disorder but a family of dissociable deficits that vary across patients and tasks. Neglect may affect perceptual exploration, internal representation, or motor intention, and can be expressed in personal, peripersonal, or extrapersonal space. These dimensions do not always co-occur, helping explain why bedside behavior can differ markedly even among patients with apparently similar lesions ref [5], ref [6].

Behavioral heterogeneity is also evident in the distinction between egocentric and allocentric neglect. Some patients omit stimuli on the contralesional side of viewer-centered space, whereas others process the left side of individual objects abnormally regardless of object position. Large cohort work has shown that these frames of reference can dissociate, with implications for assessment and treatment selection ref [7]. Performance further fluctuates with task demands, sustained attention, and arousal, so cancellation, line bisection, drawing, reading, and navigation may reveal partially different deficits rather than a single severity continuum ref [8].

An additional source of heterogeneity is the presence of associated disturbances such as extinction, anosognosia, and directional hypokinesia, which can amplify disability while remaining mechanistically separable from core neglect. Accordingly, contemporary clinical characterization emphasizes multidomain profiling over reliance on any single test, a view reinforced by standardization efforts such as the Behavioral Inattention Test ref [9].

subsections.section_title: Conceptual and Clinical Foundations of Visuospatial Neglect
subsections.content:
Visuospatial neglect is most commonly observed after stroke, particularly following right-hemisphere damage, but reported prevalence varies substantially with case mix, assessment method, and time since lesion. In unselected acute stroke cohorts, neglect is frequent and tends to be more prevalent and severe after right than left hemisphere infarction, although clinically significant left-sided neglect after left hemisphere stroke is also well documented ref [2], ref [10]. Prevalence estimates are highest in the hyperacute and acute phases and decline over time, reflecting both spontaneous recovery and the fact that milder forms may be missed without sensitive testing ref [10].

The syndrome is especially associated with lesions in the right middle cerebral artery territory and can follow cortical, subcortical, or network-level injury involving fronto-parietal, temporo-parietal, insular, thalamic, and white-matter pathways. Contemporary lesion-symptom work emphasizes that neglect is not tied to a single cortical locus but emerges from disruption of distributed attentional systems and their structural connections ref [11]. This helps explain why neglect can occur after ischemic stroke, intracerebral hemorrhage, traumatic brain injury, and less commonly brain tumors or other focal lesions.

Although stroke remains the dominant neurological context in rehabilitation settings, epidemiological synthesis also indicates that persistent neglect is clinically important because it predicts poorer motor recovery, longer inpatient stay, and reduced functional independence ref [12]. Accordingly, epidemiology in neglect is inseparable from service context: detection depends on systematic screening in stroke units and neurorehabilitation pathways, where the condition is both common and prognostically consequential.

subsections.section_title: Conceptual and Clinical Foundations of Visuospatial Neglect
subsections.content:
Visuospatial neglect has major functional consequences because it disrupts the selection and monitoring of behavior in everyday environments, not merely performance on paper-and-pencil tests. Patients may collide with objects, omit grooming or dressing on the contralesional side, fail to eat food from one half of the plate, and show impaired wheelchair navigation, transfers, and community mobility. These deficits are strongly associated with reduced independence in activities of daily living and poorer functional status during inpatient rehabilitation ref [13], ref [14].

The rehabilitation burden is amplified by the fact that neglect predicts slower and less complete recovery after stroke. Compared with patients without neglect, affected individuals typically show longer hospital stays, worse gains on functional outcome measures, and an increased likelihood of requiring institutional care or supervision after discharge ref [14], ref [15]. Because neglect can also reduce engagement with therapy tasks and awareness of deficits, it may limit the effectiveness of otherwise standard motor and occupational rehabilitation approaches.

Importantly, the impact of neglect extends beyond the acute phase. Persistent neglect is linked to long-term disability and reduced participation, even when primary motor deficits improve ref [16]. This makes systematic detection clinically essential: neglect is not simply a co-occurring cognitive sign, but a major determinant of rehabilitation complexity, caregiver burden, and resource use. Accordingly, its functional significance provides a central rationale for targeted therapeutic and neuromodulatory interventions.

subsections.section_title: Conceptual and Clinical Foundations of Visuospatial Neglect
subsections.content:
Visuospatial neglect must be distinguished from other disorders that can also produce contralesional behavioral failure. Unlike homonymous hemianopia, neglect is not reducible to a primary sensory field defect: patients may detect stimuli in the contralesional field under some conditions yet fail to orient, explore, or act toward that side in spontaneous behavior, reflecting impaired spatial attention and representation rather than only loss of visual input ref [17]. This dissociation is clinically important because standard confrontation testing may underestimate neglect, whereas cancellation, line bisection, and functional observation often reveal its characteristic context dependence.

Neglect also differs from extinction, in which contralesional stimuli are detected in isolation but missed during bilateral simultaneous stimulation; extinction can co-occur with neglect but is conceptually narrower and often less pervasive across tasks and modalities ref [18]. Similarly, allocentric object-centered neglect should be separated from egocentric neglect, and motor-intentional deficits such as directional hypokinesia can contribute to poor contralesional action without fully explaining perceptual-attentional neglect ref [19].

A further diagnostic distinction concerns anosognosia and body-representation disorders. Personal neglect, anosognosia for hemiplegia, and somatoparaphrenia frequently accompany right-hemisphere stroke, but they target the patient's own body or illness awareness rather than extrapersonal spatial exploration per se ref [20]. Careful differentiation among these syndromes is essential because they imply partially dissociable mechanisms and may require different assessment strategies and rehabilitation targets.

subsections.section_title: Theoretical Models and Neurocognitive Mechanisms
subsections.subsection_title: Attentional Imbalance and Interhemispheric Competition Models
subsections.content:
Attentional imbalance accounts propose that hemispatial neglect arises when right-hemisphere damage disrupts the normal asymmetry of spatial attention, leaving ipsilesional orienting relatively overexpressed. A foundational version of this view holds that the right hemisphere represents both hemispaces whereas the left is more strongly biased toward contralateral space, so right-sided lesions produce a particularly severe rightward attentional bias ref [21]. This framework explains why neglect is most common and enduring after right hemisphere stroke and why deficits often extend beyond simple sensory loss.

Interhemispheric competition models refined this idea by emphasizing reciprocal inhibitory interactions between homologous attentional systems. According to Kinsbourne, unilateral damage not only weakens contralesional orienting but also releases the intact hemisphere from inhibition, further amplifying ipsilesional attentional capture ref [22]. Evidence from line bisection and cueing paradigms is broadly consistent with a pathological rightward gradient of spatial priority after right hemisphere injury ref [23], while neurostimulation studies in healthy participants have shown that transiently reducing parietal excitability can induce neglect-like lateralized biases, lending causal support to competitive interhemispheric mechanisms ref [24].

Although these models do not explain all features of neglect, they remain influential because they connect behavior to large-scale dorsal frontoparietal control systems and motivate treatments aimed at rebalancing hemispheric excitability. They also provide a theoretical rationale for prism adaptation and non-invasive brain stimulation approaches designed either to enhance damaged right-hemisphere networks or suppress hyperactive left-hemisphere regions.

subsections.section_title: Theoretical Models and Neurocognitive Mechanisms
subsections.content:
Representational accounts propose that neglect can affect internal spatial models rather than only online sensory attention. Classic evidence came from patients who, when asked to imagine familiar places from memory, omitted landmarks on the contralesional side of the imagined scene despite intact knowledge of the environment, suggesting a disorder in the exploration or construction of mental representations rather than a purely perceptual deficit ref [5]. Subsequent work showed that representational neglect can occur across imagery, description, and memory-guided tasks, although its relation to perceptual neglect is variable rather than obligatory ref [25].

A complementary line of theory emphasizes defective spatial transformation. On this view, neglect may emerge when the brain fails to remap information between viewer-centered, object-centered, and action-centered coordinates, helping to explain why some patients neglect the left side of objects irrespective of where those objects appear, whereas others show body-, trunk-, or gaze-centered biases ref [26]. Neuropsychological dissociations between egocentric and allocentric neglect support this framework and indicate that neglect is not a unitary spatial disorder but a family of impairments affecting different reference frames and transformation operations ref [27].

These accounts are important because they link clinical heterogeneity to specific computational demands: generating, maintaining, and transforming spatial representations. They also predict why performance can differ sharply between copying, reading, imagery, and navigation tasks, and why treatment may need to target not only contralesional orienting but also representational exploration and coordinate transformation mechanisms.

subsections.section_title: Theoretical Models and Neurocognitive Mechanisms
subsections.content:
Although neglect is classically framed as a lateralized spatial-attention disorder, influential accounts emphasize that many patients also show deficits in tonic and phasic alertness, sustained attention, and broader capacity limitations. Robertson and colleagues argued that reduced arousal can exacerbate spatial bias by weakening the resources needed to maintain contralesional orienting, thereby helping explain fluctuations in severity across tasks and time ref [28]. Consistent with this view, right-hemisphere stroke may produce a compound syndrome in which non-spatial vigilance impairments interact with spatially selective deficits rather than merely co-occurring with them.

Empirical work supports this interactionist account. In a longitudinal study, Hjaltason et al. showed that measures of sustained attention predicted neglect severity and recovery, suggesting that vigilance is not epiphenomenal but functionally relevant to persistent impairment ref [29]. Robertson et al. further demonstrated that increasing phasic alertness with brief warning tones could transiently reduce neglect, indicating that manipulation of general arousal can rebalance spatial performance ref [30]. Such findings challenged strictly spatial theories and encouraged models in which alerting systems modulate competitive attentional selection.

Neurocognitively, these effects are often linked to right-lateralized fronto-parietal and subcortical systems that support alertness and sustained attention. Husain and Rorden proposed that neglect commonly reflects damage to interacting spatial and non-spatial components, including deficits of vigilance and attentional engagement, which may be especially relevant after right hemisphere lesions ref [31]. This perspective has important therapeutic implications: interventions that enhance arousal or reduce non-spatial attentional load may improve neglect even when they do not directly target spatial representations.

subsections.section_title: Theoretical Models and Neurocognitive Mechanisms
subsections.content:
Accounts of neglect limited to perceptual-attentional bias are insufficient to explain the frequent dissociation between defective exploration of contralesional space and relatively preserved detection under forced viewing. Sensorimotor and intentional theories therefore distinguish an impairment in generating or directing actions toward contralesional space ("aiming" neglect) from deficits in perceptual representation ("where" neglect). Clinical and experimental observations showed that patients may fail to initiate eye, head, or hand movements leftward even when sensory input is available, implying a disorder of spatially coded motor intention rather than purely degraded perception ref [32], ref [33].

This perspective was sharpened by work separating directional hypokinesia and motor extinction from sensory neglect. In directional hypokinesia, movements toward the contralesional side are disproportionately slow or reduced regardless of the limb used, suggesting that motor plans are themselves laterally biased. Such findings support the view that neglect can reflect disruption of circuits transforming spatial goals into exploratory or reaching acts, rather than a unitary visual-attentional deficit ref [34]. Related demonstrations that prism adaptation can ameliorate exploratory and action-related biases are also often interpreted within this sensorimotor framework, because visuomotor realignment may recalibrate pathological action vectors toward contralesional space ref [35].

Neuroanatomically, intentional components have been linked especially to dorsal fronto-parietal and premotor systems, basal ganglia, and their white-matter connections, complementing more posterior lesions associated with perceptual neglect. The major implication is that assessment should sample exploratory orienting, reaching, and action initiation in addition to cancellation or copying, since patients with similar bedside neglect scores may differ substantially in the balance between perceptual and motor-intentional dysfunction.

subsections.section_title: Theoretical Models and Neurocognitive Mechanisms
subsections.content:
Lesion-symptom mapping and network analyses indicate that visuospatial neglect is not reducible to damage at a single cortical locus, but instead reflects disruption of distributed right-hemisphere systems supporting orienting, target selection, and spatial working representations. Although early work emphasized the inferior parietal lobule and temporo-parietal junction, voxel-based analyses showed that neglect can follow lesions involving superior temporal, inferior frontal, and subcortical regions as well, consistent with a network disorder rather than a unitary syndrome ref [19].

This network perspective was sharpened by studies linking neglect to disconnection between large-scale attention systems. Corbetta and Shulman argued that right-lateralized ventral attention regions, particularly the temporo-parietal junction and ventral frontal cortex, interact with bilateral dorsal frontoparietal control networks to reorient attention; damage to these interactions can therefore produce persistent spatial bias ref [36]. White-matter evidence further supports this view: tractography and lesion analyses have implicated the superior longitudinal fasciculus, especially pathways linking parietal and frontal cortex, in chronic neglect severity ref [37].

Recent connectomic work suggests that behavioural heterogeneity partly reflects which components of these networks are structurally or functionally disconnected. For example, structural disconnection involving temporo-parietal and frontal pathways predicts neglect better than cortical lesion topography alone in some cohorts ref [38]. Overall, lesion correlates of neglect are best understood as damage to a right-dominant attentional network spanning cortical nodes, subcortical structures, and their connecting fibre pathways, helping explain why patients differ in perceptual, exploratory, and representational symptoms.

subsections.section_title: Theoretical Models and Neurocognitive Mechanisms
subsections.subsection_title: Implications of Theory for Treatment Design
subsections.content:
Theoretical accounts of neglect imply that treatment should be mechanism-specific rather than syndrome-based. Interhemispheric competition models motivate interventions that either upregulate damaged right-hemisphere attention networks or downregulate relatively hyperactive contralesional regions, providing a rationale for non-invasive brain stimulation paired with behavioral training ref [39]. By contrast, representational and spatial transformation accounts predict greater benefit from methods that recalibrate egocentric coordinates or sensorimotor mappings, such as prism adaptation, particularly when defective visuomotor remapping contributes to spatial bias ref [40].

Models emphasizing arousal and non-spatial deficits further suggest that some patients require restoration of tonic/phasic alertness before, or alongside, lateralized attention therapy. Pharmacological or behavioral alertness-enhancing approaches can therefore be expected to improve performance most when neglect is compounded by sustained-attention failure, rather than by a purely directional orienting deficit ref [41]. This logic also argues for multidomain assessment to identify the dominant impairment profile in each patient.

A theory-informed treatment framework consequently favors stratification and combination therapy: visual scanning may target exploratory bias, prism adaptation may address premotor and spatial remapping components, and stimulation protocols may rebalance distributed frontoparietal networks ref [40], ref [42]. The broader rehabilitation literature increasingly supports this individualized view, while also noting that variable response across patients likely reflects heterogeneity in lesion site, network disconnection, and the relative weight of spatial versus non-spatial mechanisms ref [43].

subsections.section_title: Assessment, Outcome Measurement, and Methodological Challenges
subsections.content:
Bedside and paper-and-pencil tools remain the clinical entry point for detecting visuospatial neglect because they are rapid, inexpensive, and feasible in acute stroke settings. Common tasks include line and star cancellation, line bisection, figure or scene copying, and drawing from memory. These measures sample different components of neglect rather than a unitary syndrome, and dissociations across tasks are common; for example, cancellation is often more sensitive to exploratory deficits, whereas line bisection may capture lateralized spatial bias through partly distinct mechanisms ref [44], ref [45].

Standardized batteries were developed to improve diagnostic coverage and comparability. The Behavioural Inattention Test combines conventional paper-and-pencil items with more behaviorally oriented subtests and has been widely used as a benchmark for clinical screening and research stratification ref [9]. Nonetheless, even established bedside instruments can miss mild, recovered, or context-dependent neglect, especially when patients compensate under structured testing conditions. Reviews of cancellation methods have emphasized that outcome depends not only on omission counts but also on search organization, starting position, and lateralized exploration strategy ref [46].

Accordingly, bedside assessment is best viewed as a multidimensional screening stage rather than a definitive characterization of neglect. Combining several tasks increases sensitivity across egocentric and allocentric manifestations and helps distinguish perceptual-attentional from premotor components. However, score interpretation must consider lesion side, arousal, visual field status, and task demands, all of which can influence apparent severity and contribute to heterogeneity across rehabilitation studies ref [44], ref [46].

subsections.section_title: Assessment, Outcome Measurement, and Methodological Challenges
subsections.content:
Paper-and-pencil tests are indispensable for detecting visuospatial neglect, but they incompletely capture how neglect constrains everyday behavior. Functional and ecological measures therefore aim to quantify disability in tasks such as grooming, dressing, wheelchair navigation, transfers, and spatial exploration of the environment. A central example is the Catherine Bergego Scale, a 10-item observational measure scored during activities of daily living, which was developed to index neglect in real-world contexts and has been shown to reveal deficits not always apparent on conventional cancellation or copying tasks ref [47].

Ecological assessment is particularly important because anosognosia, motor impairment, and nonspatial attentional deficits can dissociate test performance from practical independence. Validation work on the Catherine Bergego Scale has supported its sensitivity and its relevance to rehabilitation settings, while also highlighting the value of comparing therapist ratings with patients’ self-ratings to quantify unawareness of neglect-related disability ref [48]. Broader reviews of neglect assessment similarly emphasize that functional scales complement impairment-based tests by improving clinical interpretation of severity and treatment impact ref [49].

More immersive approaches extend this logic by simulating everyday spatial demands under controlled conditions. For example, virtual-reality street-crossing paradigms have demonstrated that patients with neglect show ecologically meaningful safety errors despite variable performance on standard bedside measures ref [50]. In rehabilitation research, combining observational scales, caregiver/therapist reports, and task-based ecological paradigms can therefore provide a more valid estimate of whether an intervention changes participation-relevant behavior rather than only laboratory test scores.

subsections.section_title: Assessment, Outcome Measurement, and Methodological Challenges
subsections.content:
Visuospatial neglect is not a unitary syndrome, and treatment studies are increasingly interpreted through a subtyping lens. Patients may differ along at least three clinically important axes: the spatial frame affected (egocentric vs allocentric), the domain involved (perceptual-attentional vs motor-intentional), and the reference sector emphasized (personal, peripersonal, or extrapersonal space). Classic neuropsychological work showed dissociable egocentric and allocentric neglect profiles, implying that superficially similar bedside failures may arise from different underlying impairments and may not respond equally to the same intervention ref [51].

Individualized profiling therefore requires combining tasks that sample complementary components rather than relying on a single cancellation or line-bisection score. Reviews of the syndrome have emphasized that neglect can fractionate across sensory modalities, response demands, and representational versus exploratory deficits, supporting multidimensional characterization at baseline ref [52]. Lesion-symptom mapping further reinforces this view: different neglect components have been associated with partially distinct cortical and white-matter substrates, suggesting that anatomical information can refine behavioral subtyping and help explain heterogeneity in prognosis and treatment responsiveness ref [11], ref [53].

For rehabilitation research, the practical implication is that enrollment, stratification, and outcome interpretation should be anchored to explicit neglect profiles. A patient with dominant premotor-intentional bias, for example, may not be adequately represented by tests optimized for perceptual-attentional asymmetry. Subtyping also reduces apparent inconsistency across trials by distinguishing true nonresponse from mismatch between intervention mechanism and deficit phenotype.

subsections.section_title: Assessment, Outcome Measurement, and Methodological Challenges
subsections.content:
Outcome metrics in visuospatial neglect rehabilitation must capture change at multiple levels, because improvement on impairment-based cancellation or line bisection tasks does not necessarily translate into better everyday behavior. Reviews of neglect assessment have therefore emphasized combining conventional neuropsychological tests with measures that are more sensitive to disability, participation, and transfer to daily activities ref [54]. This is especially important in intervention studies, where reliance on a single paper-and-pencil endpoint can overestimate clinically meaningful benefit.

One widely adopted strategy is to pair impairment measures with functional scales such as the Catherine Bergego Scale (CBS), which quantifies neglect during everyday activities and has shown utility both as an assessment and as a rehabilitation outcome measure ref [55]. The CBS is often complemented by summary stroke disability scales, but these broad measures may be insufficiently specific to neglect-related change. Accordingly, methodological recommendations for neglect trials have argued for multidimensional outcome batteries that distinguish between near-transfer effects on trained tasks, far-transfer effects on untrained spatial behavior, and broader gains in independence or safety ref [56].

Interpretation of outcomes also depends on timing and psychometric context. Because spontaneous recovery is substantial in the early post-stroke period, repeated measurement and appropriate controls are critical for attributing change to treatment rather than natural resolution ref [57]. In addition, treatment effects may vary by neglect subtype and by whether outcomes index perceptual-attentional versus premotor-exploratory deficits, reinforcing the need for prespecified primary endpoints and clinically anchored secondary outcomes in rehabilitation research.

subsections.section_title: Assessment, Outcome Measurement, and Methodological Challenges
subsections.content:
Marked between-study variability in visuospatial neglect research arises first from heterogeneity in case definition and sampling. Studies differ in whether they recruit acute or chronic stroke survivors, right-hemisphere only versus mixed lesion groups, and whether neglect is defined by a single cancellation task or by multidomain batteries. This is consequential because neglect is not a unitary syndrome: dissociations across personal, peripersonal, and extrapersonal space, as well as across perceptual and premotor components, mean that prevalence and treatment responsiveness depend heavily on which deficits are measured ref [58], ref [59].

A second source of variability is the mismatch between impairment-level tests and ecologically meaningful outcomes. Conventional paper-and-pencil tasks often show limited correspondence with disability in everyday activities, whereas functional measures capture broader consequences that may change on different timescales. In addition, spontaneous recovery, lesion site and size, co-occurring visual field loss or anosognosia, and differences in rehabilitation intensity can all confound interpretation of intervention effects if not explicitly controlled or stratified ref [13], ref [60].

Methodological choices further amplify inconsistency across studies. Trials vary in outcome timing, use of single versus repeated baselines, blinding procedures, and whether analyses focus on group means or clinically significant individual change. Reviews of neglect rehabilitation have repeatedly noted small samples, mixed interventions, and nonstandardized endpoints, all of which limit meta-analytic comparability and may obscure subgroup-specific benefits. Greater harmonization of diagnostic criteria, core outcome sets, and reporting standards would therefore improve both internal validity and cross-study synthesis ref [60], ref [61].

subsections.section_title: Assessment, Outcome Measurement, and Methodological Challenges
subsections.subsection_title: Methodological Issues in Clinical Trials and Systematic Reviews
subsections.content:
Clinical trials in visuospatial neglect are hindered by substantial methodological heterogeneity. Samples often mix acute and chronic stroke, right- and left-hemisphere lesions, and patients with different neglect subtypes, while using small single-center cohorts that are underpowered for subgroup analysis. Outcome assessment is likewise inconsistent: studies alternate between cancellation and line-bisection tests, functional scales, and ad hoc composite endpoints, making cross-trial comparison difficult and increasing the risk that treatment effects reflect task-specific learning rather than generalized recovery ref [62], ref [63].

Systematic reviews have repeatedly noted that many neglect intervention studies are limited by inadequate randomization procedures, poor allocation concealment, lack of blinded outcome assessment, short follow-up, and incomplete reporting of co-interventions and spontaneous recovery windows ref [62], ref [64]. These problems are especially consequential because neglect symptoms may improve rapidly in the early post-stroke period, so uncontrolled or poorly timed designs can overestimate efficacy. For rehabilitation trials, preregistered protocols, clearer stratification by neglect phenotype, and standardized core outcome sets would improve internal validity and interpretability.

Evidence synthesis faces additional challenges. Meta-analyses frequently pool interventions with different mechanisms, doses, and targets—such as prism adaptation, non-invasive brain stimulation, and visual scanning training—despite limited comparability. Reviews therefore often conclude that promising signals exist but confidence in pooled estimates remains low because of clinical and methodological heterogeneity and probable publication bias ref [64], ref [65]. More robust multicenter trials with harmonized assessment batteries and longer-term functional outcomes are essential for reducing uncertainty in future systematic reviews.

subsections.section_title: Theory-Informed Conventional and Emerging Rehabilitation Strategies
subsections.content:
Top-down attention training approaches target the voluntary control deficits that contribute to visuospatial neglect, particularly impaired orienting toward contralesional space and reduced sustained attention. Unlike primarily sensory-driven methods, these interventions rely on explicit task goals, strategy use, and repeated practice to strengthen endogenous attentional allocation. A major rationale is that neglect is exacerbated when non-spatial alertness and executive control are compromised, making training paradigms that demand monitoring, cue utilization, and deliberate exploration theoretically attractive ref [66], ref [67].

Clinical implementations have included computer-based visual scanning tasks, cancellation paradigms with feedback, cueing procedures, and more structured attention process training. Robertson and colleagues showed that enhancing tonic and phasic alertness could transiently reduce neglect manifestations, supporting models in which impaired arousal interacts with lateralized spatial bias ref [67]. Systematic work on attention training after acquired brain injury has also informed neglect rehabilitation by emphasizing graded practice of sustained, selective, and divided attention, although transfer to everyday behavior remains variable ref [68].

Evidence syntheses suggest that top-down training can improve trained tasks and some standard neglect measures, but effects are often heterogeneous and sensitive to chronicity, lesion profile, and treatment intensity. Reviews have therefore argued that strategic attention training is most promising when embedded within broader, functionally oriented rehabilitation rather than delivered as an isolated drill-based technique ref [60], ref [69].

subsections.section_title: Theory-Informed Conventional and Emerging Rehabilitation Strategies
subsections.content:
Bottom-up sensory and perceptual stimulation approaches aim to reduce visuospatial neglect by increasing the salience of contralesional inputs or transiently rebalancing orienting networks without requiring sustained strategic control. Classic examples include caloric vestibular stimulation, optokinetic stimulation, and neck-muscle vibration, each of which can induce short-lived improvements in exploratory behavior, line bisection, or personal and extrapersonal awareness by shifting egocentric reference frames or biasing attention toward neglected space ref [70], ref [71].

Among these methods, vestibular stimulation has provided particularly influential evidence that neglect is partly modifiable through peripheral sensory drives: left cold caloric stimulation can temporarily ameliorate neglect symptoms, supporting models in which multisensory bodily signals interact with spatial attention and representation ref [70]. Similarly, optokinetic stimulation, typically using leftward-moving visual patterns, is thought to entrain ipsilesional-to-contralesional orienting and has shown beneficial effects in controlled clinical studies ref [72]. Proprioceptive manipulations such as neck-muscle vibration may act through a related recalibration of trunk- or head-centered coordinates ref [71].

Clinically, these interventions are usually considered adjunctive rather than stand-alone therapies because effects are often immediate but not durable, treatment protocols remain heterogeneous, and response may depend on lesion location and neglect subtype. Nevertheless, bottom-up stimulation has been important theoretically: it demonstrates that neglect can be modulated through sensory-driven changes in spatial coding, and it has informed later multimodal rehabilitation programs that combine transient arousal or orienting gains with active training to promote longer-lasting functional generalization ref [73].

subsections.section_title: Theory-Informed Conventional and Emerging Rehabilitation Strategies
subsections.content:
Prism adaptation (PA) is the best-studied sensorimotor intervention for visuospatial neglect and is typically framed as a recalibration procedure rather than a purely attentional training method. During repeated pointing while wearing prisms that laterally displace the visual field, patients gradually reduce visuomotor error and subsequently show after-effects in the opposite direction once prisms are removed. In neglect, this recalibration is thought to modify spatial reference frames and rebalance exploratory behavior, with effects that can extend beyond the trained motor task to visual search, line bisection, and some functional activities ref [35], ref [74].

The seminal rehabilitation studies by Rossetti and colleagues demonstrated that adaptation to a rightward optical deviation could ameliorate signs of left neglect after right-hemisphere stroke, helping establish PA as a mechanistically distinctive treatment ref [35]. Subsequent work suggested that benefits may arise because adaptation engages parietal-cerebellar-premotor circuits involved in error correction and remapping, thereby influencing egocentric coding and exploratory orienting rather than simply cueing attention leftward ref [40]. This theoretical position has made PA especially important in accounts that link neglect to disrupted sensorimotor transformations and spatial priors.

At the same time, the clinical literature indicates substantial heterogeneity in response. Reviews and meta-analyses report encouraging short-term effects but variable durability and generalization, with outcomes depending on lesion characteristics, chronicity, protocol intensity, and the sensitivity of functional endpoints ref [74], ref [75]. Accordingly, PA is best regarded as a theoretically informative and clinically useful component of multimodal rehabilitation, particularly when combined with interventions targeting sustained exploration and transfer to everyday activities.

subsections.section_title: Theory-Informed Conventional and Emerging Rehabilitation Strategies
subsections.subsection_title: Eye Movement and Visual Exploration Training
subsections.content:
Eye movement and visual exploration training targets one of the most behaviorally salient features of visuospatial neglect: impoverished orienting and search toward contralesional space. These interventions typically use structured cueing, cancellation or reading tasks, and repeated scanning routines to encourage larger-amplitude saccades and more systematic leftward exploration. The theoretical rationale is primarily compensatory, aiming to strengthen voluntary attentional control and oculomotor strategies that can partially offset the pathological ipsilesional bias rather than directly normalize the underlying lesion-induced network imbalance ref [76], ref [77].

Clinical studies suggest that visual scanning training can improve performance on paper-and-pencil neglect measures and some everyday activities, especially when practice is intensive and explicitly linked to task goals. Early controlled work showed that training patients to adopt organized scanning routines reduced neglect symptoms, while later reviews concluded that benefits are most consistent for trained exploration behaviors, with more variable transfer to broader functional outcomes ref [76], ref [60]. Eye movement-based approaches have also been combined with reading-specific rehabilitation, where systematic leftward saccadic training may reduce neglect dyslexia and improve text exploration ref [78].

A key limitation is that gains often depend on sustained strategy use and may generalize incompletely outside the practiced context. For this reason, visual exploration training is often best conceptualized as a compensatory method that can be integrated with other approaches, including sensory cueing or prism-based methods, to increase ecological relevance and durability. Contemporary rehabilitation frameworks therefore emphasize embedding scanning habits into meaningful activities and monitoring whether improved ocular exploration translates into wider participation-level benefit ref [60], ref [79].

subsections.section_title: Theory-Informed Conventional and Emerging Rehabilitation Strategies
subsections.content:
Limb activation and related motor-based interventions are grounded in the observation that contralesional movement can transiently reduce neglect, presumably by increasing activation within damaged fronto-parietal and premotor-intentional networks. Early clinical work showed that voluntary movement of the neglected-side limb, particularly the left hand in right-hemisphere stroke, could improve performance on cancellation and exploratory tasks, supporting a link between motor intention and spatial attention rather than a purely sensory effect ref [80].

Subsequent studies refined this account by distinguishing active from passive movement and by emphasizing the importance of intentional motor engagement. In this framework, benefit is expected when the intervention recruits directional action planning toward contralesional space, for example through repeated reaching, hand use, or cueing protocols that encourage leftward orienting. Robertson and North provided influential evidence that limb activation can ameliorate unilateral neglect in some patients, although effects are often task-dependent and not uniformly sustained ref [81]. This mechanistic interpretation also aligns with broader analyses of premotor neglect, in which impaired initiation of contralesional actions contributes to reduced exploration and awareness of space ref [82].

Clinically, motor-based therapies are attractive because they are simple, inexpensive, and readily combined with visual scanning, prism adaptation, or task-oriented occupational therapy. However, systematic review evidence indicates that the overall efficacy base remains limited by small samples, heterogeneity of protocols, and modest data on transfer to activities of daily living ref [60]. Accordingly, limb activation is best viewed as a theoretically coherent adjunct that may be particularly useful in patients with prominent motor-intentional deficits, rather than as a stand-alone restorative treatment.

subsections.section_title: Theory-Informed Conventional and Emerging Rehabilitation Strategies
subsections.content:
Multimodal and technology-assisted rehabilitation aims to combine complementary mechanisms rather than relying on a single therapeutic lever. In visuospatial neglect, this typically involves pairing attentional training, visual exploration, sensory cueing, or sensorimotor adaptation with computerized delivery formats that increase intensity, feedback, and standardization. Reviews of neglect rehabilitation have noted that such approaches are attractive because neglect is clinically heterogeneous and often spans perceptual-attentional, representational, and motor-intentional components, making single-component interventions only partially effective ref [60].

Computer-based training has been used to scaffold repeated exploration toward contralesional space, often with adaptive task difficulty and performance feedback. Early work on virtual reality also suggested that ecologically richer environments may improve engagement and permit practice of goal-directed navigation and search behaviors that are difficult to capture with paper-and-pencil tasks alone ref [83]. More recent systems extend this logic through immersive or semi-immersive platforms, eye-tracking, and serious-game formats, with the goal of promoting transfer from structured exercises to everyday spatial behavior; however, evidence remains stronger for feasibility than for robust superiority over conventional therapy across outcomes and time points ref [84].

A related line of work combines technologies with established treatments, for example integrating prism adaptation with computer-based feedback or embedding visual scanning within dynamic multisensory interfaces. Such multimodal programs are theoretically appealing because they may jointly recalibrate spatial representations while reinforcing compensatory exploration. Nonetheless, current evidence still points to substantial variability in dosage, patient selection, and endpoint sensitivity, underscoring the need for larger controlled studies that explicitly test mechanism-specific combinations and generalization to activities of daily living ref [60], ref [85].

subsections.section_title: Theory-Informed Conventional and Emerging Rehabilitation Strategies
subsections.content:
A useful way to organize rehabilitation for visuospatial neglect is to distinguish compensatory approaches, which teach patients to strategically overcome their bias, from restorative approaches, which aim to normalize the underlying attentional or spatial representation. This distinction is clinically relevant because many interventions improve performance on trained tasks without necessarily producing broad transfer to everyday function. Reviews of treatment studies have repeatedly noted that gains are often context-dependent, and that the strongest evidence for efficacy still comes from a limited number of approaches with variable durability and ecological generalization ref [86], ref [87].

Compensatory treatments typically emphasize explicit cueing, visual scanning routines, environmental modifications, or sustained practice that helps patients adopt leftward search strategies. These methods can improve reading, cancellation, and navigation performance, but their benefits may depend on preserved awareness, therapist support, and continued strategy use. By contrast, restorative accounts have been invoked for interventions such as prism adaptation, which may recalibrate egocentric reference frames and induce more automatic changes that extend beyond the trained task, although transfer remains inconsistent across studies and outcome measures ref [87], ref [88].

Generalization therefore remains a central benchmark rather than an automatic consequence of symptom reduction. Contemporary recommendations emphasize measuring both impairment-level change and participation-level outcomes, including activities of daily living, while also considering lesion profile, chronicity, anosognosia, and co-occurring non-spatial deficits that can constrain transfer. The Catherine Bergego Scale has been especially important in this regard because it captures neglect in everyday behavior and often reveals dissociations between laboratory improvement and real-world disability ref [89], ref [90].

subsections.section_title: Therapeutic Use of Non-invasive Brain Stimulation in Visuospatial Neglect
subsections.content:
The rationale for neuromodulation in visuospatial neglect derives from network models of the syndrome rather than from a purely focal lesion account. After stroke, especially involving the right hemisphere, neglect is thought to reflect disruption of distributed fronto-parietal attention systems together with an abnormal interhemispheric imbalance: damage reduces activity in the lesioned hemisphere while leaving the contralesional hemisphere relatively disinhibited, thereby biasing spatial orienting further toward the ipsilesional side ref [19], ref [91]. This framework provides a mechanistic basis for using non-invasive brain stimulation to either upregulate residual activity in damaged attentional networks or suppress maladaptive hyperexcitability in the intact hemisphere.

The neuromodulation approach is also supported by convergent physiological evidence that attentional control depends on competitive interactions between homologous parietal regions. In healthy participants, transient perturbation of one posterior parietal cortex can induce rightward spatial bias resembling neglect, demonstrating that experimentally shifting parietal excitability is sufficient to alter spatial attention ref [92]. In patients, inhibitory stimulation over the intact left posterior parietal cortex was therefore proposed to reduce pathological interhemispheric rivalry and rebalance network function, whereas excitatory stimulation over right-hemisphere nodes aims to facilitate residual processing within damaged dorsal attention circuits ref [91], ref [93].

Importantly, this rationale aligns with contemporary lesion-network views showing that neglect severity depends on disconnection across cortical and subcortical attention networks rather than injury to a single anatomical locus. Neuromodulation is consequently attractive not only as a symptomatic intervention, but also as an adjunct to behavioral rehabilitation that may transiently increase the responsiveness of surviving networks during training ref [93], ref [94].

subsections.section_title: Therapeutic Use of Non-invasive Brain Stimulation in Visuospatial Neglect
subsections.content:
Transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) has been investigated in visuospatial neglect primarily as a means of rebalancing pathological interhemispheric interactions after unilateral stroke. Most studies have used low-frequency repetitive TMS (rTMS), typically delivered to the intact posterior parietal cortex, to reduce contralesional hyperexcitability and thereby release the damaged hemisphere from excessive transcallosal inhibition. Early proof-of-concept work showed that inhibitory stimulation over the left parietal cortex could transiently ameliorate neglect symptoms, supporting the interhemispheric competition model as a therapeutic framework ref [95], ref [96].

Subsequent clinical studies extended this approach from single-session experimental designs to short treatment courses. In particular, protocols targeting the contralesional parietal cortex with repeated 1 Hz stimulation have been associated with improvements on cancellation, line bisection, and functional neglect measures, although effects vary across lesion profiles and concomitant rehabilitation exposure ref [97]. Theta-burst stimulation has also attracted attention because continuous theta-burst stimulation can produce inhibitory after-effects with shorter administration times; in a randomized sham-controlled study, this approach yielded clinically meaningful benefit and suggested feasibility for integration into routine rehabilitation schedules ref [98].

Overall, TMS studies in neglect remain relatively small and methodologically heterogeneous, but they provide important mechanistic and translational evidence. The literature favors inhibitory stimulation of the intact parietal hemisphere over excitatory stimulation of the lesioned hemisphere, reflecting both the prominence of network-disinhibition models and practical concerns regarding lesion anatomy and cortical excitability after stroke ref [96], ref [98].

subsections.section_title: Therapeutic Use of Non-invasive Brain Stimulation in Visuospatial Neglect
subsections.subsection_title: Transcranial Direct Current and Related Electrical Stimulation Methods
subsections.content:
Transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) has been explored in visuospatial neglect as a portable, low-cost method for biasing activity within the damaged attention network or rebalancing pathological interhemispheric competition. In most studies, stimulation has targeted posterior parietal regions, using anodal tDCS to enhance excitability of the lesioned hemisphere or cathodal tDCS to suppress the contralesional hemisphere, often alongside conventional neglect therapy. Early controlled work showed that parietal tDCS can produce measurable improvements on cancellation and line bisection tasks, supporting the mechanistic relevance of hemispheric rebalancing in neglect ref [99], ref [100].

Related electrical stimulation approaches have extended this logic. Galvanic vestibular stimulation (GVS), which engages vestibular-parietal networks implicated in spatial orientation, has shown transient amelioration of neglect symptoms and has been proposed as a non-invasive means of modulating multisensory spatial representations rather than focal cortical excitability alone ref [101]. More recent studies have also combined tDCS with prism adaptation or computerized scanning training, reporting additive or facilitating effects that suggest electrical stimulation may be most useful as an adjunct to behavioral rehabilitation rather than a stand-alone intervention ref [102].

Nevertheless, the tDCS literature in neglect remains methodologically heterogeneous, with small samples, variable montages, and limited durability data. Accordingly, while electrical stimulation methods are attractive for repeated bedside use and for integration into multi-session rehabilitation protocols, their clinical value depends on refining target selection, dosing, and patient stratification according to lesion anatomy and network disruption.

subsections.section_title: Therapeutic Use of Non-invasive Brain Stimulation in Visuospatial Neglect
subsections.content:
Selection of stimulation targets in visuospatial neglect is typically grounded in network models rather than purely focal lesion anatomy. A dominant rationale comes from the interhemispheric rivalry account, which proposes that right-hemisphere damage produces pathological hyperexcitability of intact left parietal systems and an imbalance across dorsal attention networks; this framework motivated inhibitory stimulation of the contralesional posterior parietal cortex or excitatory stimulation of residual ipsilesional regions ref [103]. Although simplified, this model remains influential because neglect symptoms often reflect disturbed competition within distributed fronto-parietal circuits rather than damage to a single cortical node.

Anatomically, the intraparietal sulcus, inferior parietal lobule, and temporo-parietal junction have been the principal cortical targets, given their roles in spatial orienting and salience-driven reorienting. Lesion-mapping studies indicate that severe and persistent neglect is especially associated with damage involving perisylvian fronto-parietal white matter and disconnection between parietal and frontal attention systems, suggesting that stimulation effects may depend on the integrity of surviving network pathways rather than on target location alone ref [104], ref [105]. This supports individualized targeting based on structural imaging, lesion extent, and the presumed balance between dorsal and ventral attention network dysfunction.

Network-level considerations also argue for moving beyond single-site stimulation. Functional imaging has shown that neglect can involve abnormal activity and connectivity in bilateral attention networks, visual cortex, and remote intact areas, with recovery paralleling re-normalization of large-scale network interactions ref [19]. Accordingly, the most plausible therapeutic targets may be those capable of reweighting whole-network dynamics—either by suppressing maladaptive contralesional dominance or by facilitating residual ipsilesional hubs and their connectivity to frontal control regions ref [106].

subsections.section_title: Therapeutic Use of Non-invasive Brain Stimulation in Visuospatial Neglect
subsections.content:
Protocol design in neglect trials has varied substantially, but several recurring parameters shape interpretation of efficacy. Repetitive TMS studies have most often used inhibitory low-frequency stimulation (typically 1 Hz) over the contralesional posterior parietal cortex, delivered for brief daily sessions across several consecutive days, reflecting the interhemispheric competition model and the need to accumulate effects beyond a single session ref [107], ref [108]. By contrast, tDCS protocols have included both cathodal stimulation of the intact hemisphere and anodal stimulation of ipsilesional regions, usually at low currents applied for 10–20 minutes and combined with behavioral training, with the montage selected according to whether the goal is to suppress maladaptive hyperactivity or facilitate damaged attentional networks ref [109].

Treatment timing is equally consequential. Early post-stroke intervention is theoretically attractive because network reorganization is most dynamic during the subacute period, yet spontaneous recovery and medical instability complicate attribution of benefit. Chronic-stage studies provide cleaner estimates of stimulation-specific effects, but may underestimate responsiveness of partially preserved networks. Reviews of the clinical literature therefore emphasize that session number, spacing, and coupling with conventional neglect therapy are not minor methodological details but central determinants of outcome magnitude and durability ref [110].

A practical implication is that neuromodulation should be conceptualized less as a single stand-alone exposure than as a dosed rehabilitation adjunct. Available studies suggest that repeated-session schedules and online pairing with visuospatial training are more plausible routes to durable change than isolated stimulation, although the field still lacks consensus on optimal intensity, total dose, and the ideal post-stroke window for different neglect phenotypes ref [108], ref [110].

subsections.section_title: Therapeutic Use of Non-invasive Brain Stimulation in Visuospatial Neglect
subsections.subsection_title: Clinical Efficacy and Durability of Effects
subsections.content:
Clinical efficacy data for non-invasive brain stimulation in visuospatial neglect remain promising but heterogeneous. Early controlled studies suggested that inhibitory repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) over the intact posterior parietal cortex can improve cancellation performance, line bisection, and other neglect measures beyond sham, supporting a therapeutic effect consistent with interhemispheric rebalancing models ref [111], ref [112]. Similar short-term benefits have been reported with theta-burst protocols, although outcomes vary across lesion sites, chronicity, and concomitant rehabilitation intensity ref [113].

The durability of these gains is less firmly established than their immediate effects. Single-session studies often show transient improvements measured over minutes to days, whereas repeated-session protocols are more likely to yield effects that persist for several weeks, particularly when stimulation is paired with behavioral training ref [112], ref [113]. Nevertheless, the literature is dominated by small samples and variable endpoints, making it difficult to determine whether improvements generalize from paper-and-pencil tests to sustained functional gains in activities of daily living.

Meta-analytic and systematic review evidence therefore supports a cautious interpretation: non-invasive stimulation appears capable of augmenting neglect rehabilitation, but effect sizes are sensitive to protocol design and study quality, and long-term follow-up data remain sparse ref [114], ref [115]. Future trials need adequately powered designs, standardized outcome batteries, and longer follow-up intervals to clarify clinical durability and identify the patients most likely to benefit.

subsections.section_title: Therapeutic Use of Non-invasive Brain Stimulation in Visuospatial Neglect
subsections.content:
Across non-invasive brain stimulation studies in visuospatial neglect, safety findings have generally been favorable when standard screening and dosing guidelines are followed. For repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS), reported adverse events are usually mild and transient, most commonly scalp discomfort, headache, or fatigue; the main serious theoretical risk remains seizure, which is rare under guideline-concordant protocols ref [116], ref [117]. For transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS), tolerability is typically high, with itching, tingling, erythema, or mild burning sensations at the electrode site representing the most frequent complaints ref [118].

In stroke populations, feasibility is shaped not only by device safety but also by neurological and medical complexity. Neglect patients may have reduced endurance, impaired awareness, communication deficits, or difficulty maintaining stable positioning, all of which can affect session completion and protocol adherence. Nonetheless, published rehabilitation studies indicate that both rTMS and tDCS can be implemented at the bedside or in outpatient settings with acceptable dropout rates and without major interference with concurrent therapy when appropriate monitoring is used ref [119], ref [120].

Practical safeguards are especially important in this group: exclusion of patients with seizure risk factors or incompatible implants, careful review of medications, gradual familiarization with stimulation sensations, and coordination with rehabilitation schedules. Overall, current evidence supports non-invasive brain stimulation as a feasible adjunct to neglect rehabilitation, but larger trials should report adverse events systematically and include longer follow-up to better characterize cumulative burden, delayed effects, and tolerability in frailer stroke survivors.

subsections.section_title: Evidence Synthesis, Clinical Translation, and Future Directions
subsections.content:
Across intervention classes, non-invasive brain stimulation should be compared less by nominal modality than by target engagement, effect size, and compatibility with concurrent rehabilitation. Repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) and transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) remain the most studied approaches after stroke, but systematic reviews consistently indicate modest average benefits with substantial heterogeneity across impairment domains, stages of recovery, and stimulation parameters ref [121], ref [122]. This pattern suggests that apparent differences between classes often reflect protocol optimization and patient selection rather than a simple hierarchy of efficacy.

Mechanistically, high-frequency ipsilesional excitation and low-frequency contralesional inhibition via rTMS offer stronger spatial focality and clearer physiological readouts, whereas tDCS provides lower-intensity, more portable modulation that is easier to pair with training. Comparative syntheses have therefore tended to favor a pragmatic view: rTMS may be preferable when precise cortical targeting and larger instantaneous effects are desired, while tDCS may be advantageous for scalable, repeated adjunctive use during task practice ref [122], ref [123]. However, meta-analytic evidence does not support universal superiority of one class across all motor outcomes, and the interhemispheric competition framework that motivated many inhibitory-versus-excitatory comparisons is itself increasingly recognized as incomplete ref [124].

For clinical translation, the key comparison is not only between stimulation classes but between stimulation-alone and stimulation-plus-therapy models. Reviews of upper-limb rehabilitation indicate that gains are more consistent when neuromodulation is embedded within structured motor practice, robotics, or task-oriented therapy than when delivered in isolation ref [121], ref [125]. Future comparative work should therefore prioritize head-to-head, biomarker-stratified trials that harmonize dose, timing, and behavioral context rather than continuing to compare highly heterogeneous protocols under broad modality labels.

subsections.section_title: Evidence Synthesis, Clinical Translation, and Future Directions
subsections.content:
A central limitation of non-invasive brain stimulation (NIBS) in rehabilitation is that average treatment effects often mask substantial inter-individual variability. Precision rehabilitation therefore requires moving beyond lesion-agnostic, one-size-fits-all protocols toward patient stratification based on impairment severity, lesion topology, corticospinal tract integrity, and residual network capacity. In stroke, the proportional recovery literature and subsequent critiques together suggest that baseline motor status and available descending pathways constrain both spontaneous recovery and responsiveness to intervention, making initial phenotype definition a prerequisite for rational NIBS selection rather than a post hoc analytic variable ref [126], ref [127].

Mechanistic models of post-stroke reorganization further support individualized targeting. The bimodal balance-recovery model argues that the value of suppressing contralesional regions versus facilitating ipsilesional networks depends on the degree of structural reserve; patients with limited reserve may rely on compensatory recruitment, whereas those with preserved substrate may benefit from restoring more canonical interhemispheric dynamics ref [128]. This framework aligns with evidence that biomarkers such as motor evoked potentials and corticospinal tract injury can partition patients into biologically meaningful subgroups with different recovery trajectories and treatment windows ref [129].

In practice, precision rehabilitation should integrate multimodal profiling—clinical impairment, neurophysiology, and imaging—to guide stimulation montage, dose, and timing. Consensus recommendations for recovery prediction already emphasize combining simple bedside measures with biomarkers to improve stratification and trial enrichment, a strategy that could reduce heterogeneity and increase the probability of detecting true NIBS effects in both explanatory and pragmatic studies ref [130].

subsections.section_title: Evidence Synthesis, Clinical Translation, and Future Directions
subsections.content:
A consistent theme in non-invasive brain stimulation (NIBS) for rehabilitation is that stimulation is unlikely to be maximally effective as a stand-alone intervention; rather, it appears to act as a plasticity-gating tool whose effects depend on concurrent behavioral training. This logic is especially relevant in stroke and motor recovery, where stimulation paired with task-specific practice may reinforce use-dependent synaptic change more effectively than either component alone. Early clinical work combining repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) with intensive occupational therapy reported functional gains beyond routine care, helping establish the feasibility of stimulation-plus-training models in chronic stroke ref [131].

Evidence synthesis has reinforced both the promise and the contingency of these synergistic approaches. Reviews of tDCS in post-stroke motor recovery have concluded that benefits are more plausible when stimulation is embedded within structured therapy, but also that effects vary with lesion characteristics, timing, dosage, and the behavioral context in which stimulation is delivered ref [132]. More broadly, mechanistic and clinical reviews have argued that NIBS should be integrated with robotic therapy, constraint-induced practice, mirror therapy, gait training, or speech-language interventions according to the targeted network and learning stage, rather than applied in a one-size-fits-all manner ref [133].

The next step is to move from simple co-administration to explicitly designed synergistic models. This includes state-dependent stimulation delivered during active training, sequential priming paradigms, and multimodal protocols that combine NIBS with pharmacological or neurofeedback-based modulation. A framework for such combinatorial rehabilitation emphasizes matching stimulation polarity, site, and timing to the underlying impairment mechanism and to biomarkers of residual network capacity ref [125]. In practice, the field still needs adequately powered trials that compare specific combinations head-to-head and test whether synergy is additive, supra-additive, or limited to biologically defined subgroups.

subsections.section_title: Evidence Synthesis, Clinical Translation, and Future Directions
subsections.content:
A central barrier to evidence synthesis in non-invasive brain stimulation for rehabilitation is persistent methodological heterogeneity. Studies vary widely in montage, dose, timing relative to training, sham design, outcome selection, and lesion characterization, making between-study comparisons difficult and inflating apparent inconsistency. Consensus-oriented reporting frameworks therefore remain essential. For transcranial direct current stimulation, the methodological guidance articulated by Bikson and colleagues provides a practical minimum standard for documenting electrode placement, current intensity, session duration, device characteristics, and adverse events, all of which are necessary for reproducibility and meaningful meta-analysis ref [134].

Equivalent standardization is needed for transcranial magnetic stimulation, where effects depend strongly on coil geometry, targeting approach, stimulation intensity definition, and intersession reliability. The international safety and application guidelines from Rossi et al. and the broader recommendations on therapeutic use from Lefaucheur et al. offer a foundation for harmonized reporting, including stimulation parameters, contraindication screening, and clinical endpoints ref [116], ref [135]. Beyond technical parameters, rehabilitation trials should prespecify mechanistic and functional primary outcomes, report concomitant therapies in detail, and distinguish impairment-level gains from activity and participation effects.

Future reporting priorities should move beyond checklist compliance toward interoperable datasets that capture moderators of response, including chronicity, structural lesion burden, corticospinal tract integrity, baseline network status, and medication exposure. The call for rigor and reproducibility in brain stimulation research by Bestmann et al. is especially relevant here: adequately powered designs, transparent analytic pipelines, and reporting of null findings are prerequisites for cumulative science and for the development of precision rehabilitation models ref [136].

subsections.section_title: Evidence Synthesis, Clinical Translation, and Future Directions
subsections.content:
Long-term recovery remains a critical test for non-invasive brain stimulation (NIBS) in neurorehabilitation, because short-term gains observed in controlled trials do not always translate into durable functional change in daily life. Evidence from large pragmatic rehabilitation studies suggests that recovery trajectories extend well beyond the early subacute window and are strongly shaped by dose, task specificity, and continued practice, implying that NIBS is most likely to show lasting value when embedded within sustained rehabilitation pathways rather than delivered as an isolated procedure ref [1]. This perspective also aligns with work emphasizing the importance of measuring participation-level and quality-of-life outcomes, not only impairment-based endpoints.

Real-world implementation further depends on feasibility, treatment adherence, and integration with routine service delivery. Home- and community-oriented models are increasingly relevant, particularly for chronic stroke and other long-term disabling conditions, but they require simplified protocols, caregiver support, and monitoring strategies that preserve safety while accommodating variable environments. Importantly, implementation science lessons from rehabilitation technology indicate that efficacy alone is insufficient; adoption is influenced by workflow compatibility, patient burden, and reimbursement structures ref [2]. For NIBS, these issues are amplified by the need for repeated sessions and trained supervision.

Future progress therefore requires longer follow-up, pragmatic trial designs, and hybrid effectiveness-implementation studies. Consensus recommendations for stroke recovery research have already highlighted the need for standardized timing, clinically meaningful outcomes, and attention to contextual factors that determine whether interventions can scale across health systems ref [3]. In parallel, emerging remotely supervised stimulation frameworks may help extend dose and accessibility, but their long-term comparative effectiveness remains to be established ref [4].

subsections.section_title: Evidence Synthesis, Clinical Translation, and Future Directions
subsections.content:
Emerging research is shifting non-invasive brain stimulation (NIBS) from protocol standardization toward adaptive, mechanism-informed intervention design. A major frontier is closed-loop stimulation, in which stimulation timing or dose is adjusted using ongoing neural or behavioral signals rather than fixed schedules. This direction is motivated by evidence that brain-state dependence strongly shapes stimulation effects and may explain part of the variability seen across rehabilitation trials ref [137]. Related work in personalized connectomics further suggests that lesion location alone is insufficient; instead, distributed network topology and residual structural-functional integrity may provide more actionable targets for stimulation-assisted recovery ref [138].

Another important frontier is multimodal biomarker integration. Combining EEG, MRI-based connectivity, neurophysiology, and digital phenotyping could enable stratification of patients by recovery mechanism, treatment responsiveness, and optimal intervention window. In parallel, computational electric-field modeling is increasingly being used to individualize electrode placement and current distribution, moving beyond scalp-based heuristics toward anatomically grounded dosing ref [139]. These developments align with a broader precision-rehabilitation framework in which stimulation parameters are tailored to impairment subtype, network disruption, and task context rather than diagnosis alone.

Finally, future translational progress will likely depend on interventions that are not only personalized but also scalable and ecologically valid. Home-based and remotely supervised stimulation platforms are being actively investigated, particularly when paired with telerehabilitation and continuous outcome capture through wearable or app-based systems ref [140]. Across these avenues, the central challenge is to integrate mechanistic rigor with pragmatic trial design so that next-generation NIBS approaches improve both efficacy and real-world implementability.
